methodological_rigor.justification: This is a retrospective single-center diagnostic study of 150 patients undergoing prostate MRI followed by combined systematic and MRI-targeted transperineal biopsy, using biopsy histopathology as the reference standard and defining csPCa as Gleason >=7. Key limitations are single-site design, a single expert radiologist reader, and an enriched high-prevalence cohort (96/150 csPCa; only 16/150 negative MRI exams), which constrains generalizability and may inflate apparent performance. The statistical plan is appropriate for diagnostic accuracy comparisons (sensitivity/specificity with likelihood ratios at PI-RADS thresholds >=3 and >=4, McNemar testing for paired comparisons, and correlation/paired testing for measurement agreement).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study evaluates a clinically relevant diagnostic-support question (AI vs expert interpretation for csPCa detection on MRI) with a defined reference standard, which aligns with an individual cohort-style diagnostic accuracy design rather than mechanistic work. Clinical relevance is high because results speak directly to biopsy decision support and the ability to rule out csPCa (reported emphasis on very low NLRs) in real-world MRI workflows. However, the cohort is high-suspicion and single-center, so external validity to screening/low-risk settings remains unproven.

reporting_quality.justification: As a diagnostic accuracy comparison using a reference standard, STARD is the most applicable reporting standard; the manuscript clearly specifies patient selection/exclusions, index tests (radiologist PI-RADS v2.1 and PAROS on biparametric sequences), reference standard, thresholds (>=3 and >=4), and paired statistical comparisons. It also explicitly notes key limitations such as inability to perform per-lesion biopsy localization and the single-reader, single-scanner design. No public release of data, code, or model outputs is described in the normalized text, so reproducibility is limited to methodological description.

novelty_literature.justification: Comparing an AI tool (trial precommercial PAROS) against an experienced radiologist on csPCa detection with biopsy reference is a meaningful but increasingly common evaluation pattern in prostate MRI. The manuscript adds incremental value via a paired comparison at clinically used PI-RADS thresholds and discussion of workflow implications (rule-out use case), but it is not a first-in-class method or paradigm change. Use of a pre-launch software version further limits the long-term novelty of the specific performance numbers.

writing_presentation.justification: The paper is well organized, with clear definitions (csPCa, thresholds) and a methods section that aligns with the reported diagnostic metrics. Results are presented in a clinically interpretable way (sensitivity/specificity and likelihood ratios, plus paired significance testing) and the discussion appropriately highlights limitations such as cohort enrichment and single-center design. The abstract is quantitative and consistent with the main findings and conclusions.

key_strengths: Clinically anchored diagnostic accuracy comparison against biopsy reference with pre-specified PI-RADS thresholds (>=3, >=4) and paired statistical testing (McNemar).
Clear articulation of the tool’s likely utility as decision support, particularly for rule-out performance emphasized via low negative likelihood ratios.
key_concerns: Single-center, single-expert-reader design and highly enriched prevalence (96/150 csPCa; few negative MRIs) limit external validity, especially for screening/low-prevalence use cases.
Index tests are not strictly matched (AI on biparametric sequences vs radiologist on full multiparametric including DCE), introducing potential bias.
Per-lesion accuracy cannot be assessed due to biopsy localization constraints when multiple lesions are present, limiting granular evaluation.
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodology and reporting are strong for a retrospective diagnostic study, but generalizability and test-input mismatch are substantial; it could reach a tier-2 venue after major revisions focused on calibration/external validation framing and clearer bias analysis.
